title: Maybe God Isn’t Withholding a Better Life. Maybe You’ve Become Blind to the Life Already in Your Hands.
paragraphs: Maybe God Isn’t Withholding a Better Life. Maybe You’ve Become Blind to the Life Already in Your Hands.
Comparison keeps pointing at what is missing. Gratitude quietly opens your eyes to what grace has already placed within reach.
There is a frightening kind of poverty that can happen while your hands are still full.
You can have food on the table and feel deprived.
You can have people who love you and feel forgotten.
You can wake up breathing, walking, thinking, praying—and spend the entire morning grieving a life that belongs to somebody else.
That is what comparison can do.
It does not always steal the gift.
Sometimes it simply steals your ability to see the gift.
And perhaps that is why these words from Paul are more confronting than they first appear:
“Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.”
—1 Thessalonians 5:16–18
In Greek, the heart of the passage reads:
“Πάντοτε χαίρετε, ἀδιαλείπτως προσεύχεσθε, ἐν παντὶ εὐχαριστεῖτε…”
Pántote chaírete, adialeíptōs proseúchesthe, en pantì eucharisteîte…
“Always rejoice. Continually pray. In everything give thanks.”
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say everything that happens to you is good.
It does not tell a grieving mother to call death good.
It does not tell the betrayed spouse to call betrayal good.
It does not command the wounded to pretend they are not bleeding.
It does not require you to celebrate abuse, injustice, sickness, loss, loneliness, or sin.
Paul says, “ἐν παντὶ”—en panti—“in everything,” or “in every circumstance,” give thanks.
There is an enormous difference between thanking God for evil and remaining thankful in the presence of suffering.
Christian gratitude is not emotional dishonesty.
It is spiritual sight.
It is looking at a broken world without looking away from a faithful God.
And some of us have slowly lost that sight.
Not because God stopped giving.
Because comparison trained our eyes to notice everything except what He gave us.
Think about how easily it happens.
You once prayed for the job you now complain about every morning.
You once desperately wanted somebody to love you, and now the person beside you receives the exhausted leftovers of your attention.
You once prayed for children, and now the noise that proves they are alive sometimes feels like an interruption.
You once begged God to get you through a season you thought would destroy you.
He did.
But because another struggle arrived afterward, you barely remember that you survived.
You wanted a home.
Now you notice its imperfections.
You wanted transportation.
Now you notice what somebody else drives.
You wanted opportunity.
Now somebody else’s success makes yours feel embarrassingly small.
You wanted healing.
Then, once the pain faded, ordinary life became ordinary again.
And perhaps the saddest part is this:
Some of the things boring you today would have brought you to tears five years ago.
Read that again.
Somewhere in your past is a version of you who would look at something in your present life and whisper,
“God…You actually did it.”
But present-you barely notices anymore.
That is the tragedy of spiritual familiarity.
Mercies become furniture.
Miracles become routine.
People become background noise.
Daily bread becomes “just bread.”
And another person’s highlight reel becomes the measuring stick by which you declare your own life insufficient.
Comparison rarely walks into your heart announcing itself as idolatry.
It sounds much more reasonable.
“Why can’t my marriage look like theirs?”
“Why am I still struggling financially?”
“Why is her ministry growing faster?”
“Why did he get promoted?”
“Why does their family seem so happy?”
“Why does everybody else appear to be moving forward while I’m still here?”
And underneath all those questions, another question sometimes begins forming.
One we may be afraid to say aloud.
“God…why wasn’t what You gave me better?”
There it is.
Not always.
Not every desire for change is sinful. Scripture gives us room to lament, ask, seek, work, grow, and bring our needs honestly before God. Wanting improvement is not automatically ingratitude.
But comparison can corrupt a legitimate desire until desire becomes accusation.
Until someone else’s blessing starts looking like evidence that God has neglected you.
Until you cannot enjoy your portion because you are staring at theirs.
Until “I would like something different” becomes “What God has given me cannot possibly be enough.”
That is when comparison becomes dangerous.
Because eventually you are no longer merely comparing possessions.
You are questioning Providence.
You are quietly putting God on trial.
And social media can pour gasoline on that fire.
You wake up feeling reasonably content.
Then you scroll.
Somebody is getting married.
Somebody bought a house.
Somebody is traveling.
Somebody lost weight.
Somebody’s business exploded.
Somebody’s ministry reached thousands.
Somebody’s children look perfectly behaved.
Somebody is standing beside a new car holding an oversized ribbon.
Somebody posts the anniversary photograph with the caption about marrying their best friend.
Twenty minutes later, nothing in your physical life has changed.
Same room.
Same spouse.
Same income.
Same body.
Same calling.
Same breakfast.
Yet somehow you feel poorer.
What happened?
You consumed hundreds of fragments of other people’s lives and unconsciously assembled them into one imaginary person whose life seems better than yours in every category.
You compared your ordinary Tuesday to everybody else’s most photographable moments.
And your soul lost.
Because comparison is a game with no finish line.
There will always be someone with more.
More money.
More beauty.
More influence.
More opportunities.
More recognition.
A seemingly easier marriage.
A bigger platform.
A healthier body.
A more impressive testimony.
A nicer home.
Even if you somehow surpassed the person you envy today, comparison would simply introduce you to someone else tomorrow.
That is why comparison never finally says,
“Enough.”
But gratitude can.
Gratitude looks at daily bread and remembers that bread is mercy.
It looks at an imperfect spouse and remembers that covenant is sacred.
It hears children laughing—or crying, arguing, running through the house—and remembers that life itself is astonishing.
It wakes up with bills and remembers there is still a God to pray to.
It looks into an aging face and realizes those lines mean years were given.
It sits at a modest table and realizes Jesus never taught His disciples to pray for somebody else’s banquet.
He taught them:
“Give us this day our daily bread.”
Not tomorrow’s luxury.
Not our neighbor’s portion.
Daily bread.
Enough grace for today.
Enough mercy for today.
Enough Christ for today.
And this is where the Gospel exposes something even deeper.
Our greatest gift was never supposed to be the perfect circumstances.
Our greatest gift is Christ Himself.
If Christianity becomes merely a method for obtaining the lifestyle we envy, then we have missed Christianity entirely.
Jesus did not bleed on a cross so you could finally compete successfully with somebody on Facebook.
He came because our deepest poverty was not that somebody else had more than us.
Our deepest poverty was sin.
We needed reconciliation with God.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed a righteousness we could never manufacture.
We needed resurrection.
We needed grace.
And Christ came.
The sinless Son of God entered our brokenness, bore sin at the cross, died, and rose again.
The scandal of the Gospel is that guilty sinners are invited into grace not because we became impressive enough, but because Jesus was sufficient.
Repentance means turning from sin and returning to God.
Faith means trusting Christ rather than ourselves.
Grace means the story does not have to end where our failure says it should.
And suddenly gratitude becomes much bigger than saying, “Thank You for my house.”
It becomes:
“Jesus, thank You that I belong to You.”
“Thank You that my sins can be forgiven.”
“Thank You that shame does not get the final word.”
“Thank You that my failures do not outrank Your mercy.”
“Thank You that even when my circumstances are not what I hoped for, the cross has already proven that I am not abandoned.”
This is why biblical gratitude can coexist with tears.
You can grieve and give thanks.
You can be disappointed and give thanks.
You can want your circumstances to change and give thanks.
You can sit beside a hospital bed and still whisper the name of Jesus.
You can be uncertain about tomorrow while worshiping God today.
Paul’s command was never shallow positivity.
“Πάντοτε χαίρετε.”
Always rejoice.
“ἀδιαλείπτως προσεύχεσθε.”
Pray continually.
“ἐν παντὶ εὐχαριστεῖτε.”
In everything give thanks.
And then Paul anchors it:
“τοῦτο γὰρ θέλημα θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ εἰς ὑμᾶς.”
“For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.”
Notice where the Christian life is located.
ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
En Christō Iēsou.
In Christ Jesus.
Not in perfect circumstances.
Not in somebody else’s lifestyle.
Not in finally possessing everything you thought would make you happy.
In Christ Jesus.
Maybe you need to put the phone down tonight.
Walk through your home slowly.
Look around.
Not at what needs upgrading.
At what remains.
Listen for the voices you have become accustomed to hearing.
Look at the face you have become accustomed to seeing.
Think about the prayers God answered so gradually that you forgot they were prayers.
Remember the doors He closed that later protected you.
Remember the nights you thought you would not survive.
Remember the sin He forgave.
Remember the people He sent.
Remember the strength that appeared when yours disappeared.
Remember Calvary.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember Jesus.
Maybe your life is not as empty as comparison has been telling you.
Maybe you have simply been staring through a window into everybody else’s house while forgetting to turn around and see what grace placed inside yours.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You have been angry with your life lately.
Nothing seems enough.
You keep imagining that peace is waiting somewhere else—with another income, another body, another relationship, another city, another level of success.
But perhaps tonight the Holy Spirit is not merely asking what you want next.
Perhaps He is exposing what you stopped thanking God for.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we stop hiding what is happening inside us.
Someone else reading may desperately need to discover they are not the only believer struggling to remain grateful.
Then do something more difficult.
Before you sleep tonight, thank God specifically for five things you have stopped noticing.
Not impressive things.
Ordinary things.
A person.
A meal.
A conversation.
A place to rest.
Another morning.
The ability to pray.
Another opportunity to repent.
Another day in which the door of grace is still open.
We glorify God through faith, obedience, love, worship, truth, generosity, and lives surrendered to Christ.
But if this truth helped you see His goodness again, sharing it can become one simple act of witness.
Someone may need these words tonight.
Send this to the believer who keeps saying, “I’m behind.”
Send it to the friend whose heart has been exhausted by comparison.
The Gospel cannot be purchased, and God’s grace is not for sale.
Jesus is not merchandise.
Grace is not a transaction.
The forgiveness of sins is offered through Jesus Christ, and the proper response to the Gospel is repentance and faith.
So tonight, before you ask God why you do not have somebody else’s life, look again at the life already in your hands.
Maybe there is something there you stopped seeing.
Maybe there is someone there you stopped appreciating.
Maybe there is mercy there that became so familiar you started calling it ordinary.
Maybe God is still changing things you cannot see.
Maybe the chapter you resent is not the final chapter.
And maybe the God who met you in your scandal is still writing grace into places you thought were ruined beyond redemption.
Because comparison says:
“Look what you’re missing.”
But gratitude whispers:
“Look what God has carried you through.”
Comparison says:
“Their life is better.”
The Gospel says:
“Christ is yours.”
Comparison keeps your eyes moving sideways.
Grace lifts them toward Jesus.
So rejoice.
Pray.
Give thanks.
Not because everything is easy.
Not because everything is good.
Not because you must pretend the pain does not hurt.
But because even inside an unfinished life, Christ remains faithful.
And if you know someone whose eyes have become so fixed on what they lack that they can no longer recognize what God has already placed in their hands, share this with them.
Perhaps tonight you are not the only person God wants to remind.
Perhaps the article you almost scrolled past becomes the truth somebody else desperately needed you to pass along.
And when comparison returns tomorrow—and it probably will—come back and read this again.
Remember.
Give thanks.
Then look at your life one more time.
Not through the eyes of envy.
Through the eyes of grace.
Because one of the saddest ways to lose a blessing is never to lose it at all—but to become so accustomed to grace that you can no longer see what you are holding.
